title: The application of chatbot as an L2 writing practice tool
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a chatbot-based writing practice tool can improve second-language (L2) writing performance for young learners and how students perceive using such a tool. The study responds to a gap in prior chatbot research by testing direct comparative evidence against a non-AI instructional comparator in an elementary school context, rather than only describing feasibility or user attitudes.

The intervention was a chatbot built with Google Dialogflow and manually encoded with expressions from a Grade 5 Korean English textbook. It was designed as a conversational partner for controlled, scenario-based writing practice tied to classroom lessons. The comparison condition received traditional teacher-led writing instruction and textbook-based sentence completion/writing activities. Both groups were taught by the same teacher and used the same textbook over a 15-week period, but only the experimental group used the chatbot for individual writing practice at the end of lessons.

Participants were 75 fifth-grade elementary school students in South Korea, randomly assigned to control and experimental groups. Outcomes included pretest and posttest writing scores, rated holistically by trained raters, plus a survey of experimental-group students’ perceptions of the chatbot. The authors found no significant baseline difference between groups, but the chatbot group performed significantly better on the posttest, even after controlling for pretest scores with ANCOVA. Survey results suggested that students generally found the chatbot useful for reviewing what they learned and felt relatively comfortable using it, although perceptions of its human-likeness and effectiveness were moderate rather than strong.

The study concludes that chatbot-mediated writing practice can support young L2 learners’ writing performance and reduce anxiety by providing a less face-threatening environment than teacher-led practice. The paper also notes that the controlled, textbook-based design may be especially suitable for elementary EFL contexts where learners have limited exposure to English and limited opportunities for individualized practice.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A chatbot-based AI writing practice tool built with Google Dialogflow and scenario-based dialogue, used as an L2 language-learning conversational partner.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by Korean fifth-grade elementary students for individual English writing practice over 15 weeks, compared against traditional teacher-led writing instruction.

findings.finding_summary: In the posttest, the experimental group using the chatbot scored significantly higher than the control group receiving traditional writing instruction. The paper reports a posttest mean of 2.11 for the experimental group versus 1.74 for the control group (n=37 vs. n=38), with Mann-Whitney U = 876.50, p < .05; ANCOVA also found a significant treatment effect controlling for pretest scores (F=7.014, p=0.010).
findings.measure: Holistic English writing test scores (pretest and posttest); ANCOVA-adjusted posttest scores

findings.finding_summary: The experimental group reported generally favorable perceptions of the chatbot as a writing practice tool. Mean ratings indicated it was helpful for reviewing what was learned at school (M=3.54, n=37) and that students generally did not feel nervous when using it (M=2.14 for the nervousness item, where lower scores indicate disagreement).
findings.measure: Perception survey on chatbot usefulness, comfort, anxiety, and perceived improvement

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized two-group intervention with pretest-posttest comparison and ANCOVA, providing reasonably strong causal evidence for a specific educational chatbot. Some concerns remain because the posttest prompt differed from the pretest and the outcome was a short holistic writing score rather than a standardized measure.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported treatment effect on posttest writing performance is statistically significant, and the adjusted mean difference is moderate in practical terms (2.13 vs. 1.72 on a 0-3 scale). However, the paper does not report a standardized effect size, so the magnitude is best characterized as modest to moderate.
